title: Competition law basics
subtitle: Articles 101 and 102 TFEU, and the UK mirror that actually governs you now
objectives: State the prohibitions in Articles 101 and 102 TFEU and explain what each is designed to catch
Map each TFEU provision onto its Competition Act 1998 equivalent and identify which regime actually applies in the UK today
Apply the cartel and abuse-of-dominance concepts to a new fact pattern under the current UK regime

leadingAuthorities.role: The EU-law model for anti-competitive agreements and abuse of dominance

leadingAuthorities.citation: Consten and Grundig v Commission [1966] ECR 299
leadingAuthorities.role: Early, wide reading of 'agreement' and 'restriction of competition' under (what is now) Article 101
Defines dominance and its abuse under (what is now) Article 102
The current, CMA-enforced UK prohibitions, drafted to mirror Articles 101 and 102

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: This lesson has a trap built into its own subject matter: the EU law is history, but the domestic law that copied it is live and enforced right now by the CMA. Where the profile shows knowledge ahead of application, this note appears: 'You can probably recite the tests — the harder skill here is knowing which regime you're actually being asked about.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on the definitions before. The test pool here leans on scenarios that require you to say which regime — UK, EU-historical, or both — actually governs the facts given.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Slow down through Parts 1 and 2 before the comparative material in Part 3 — you need Articles 101 and 102 solid before the CA 1998 mapping will make sense.

overview.hook: Two rules, one used to bind the UK and no longer does; the other was written to look almost exactly like it and binds the UK today. If you can't tell a CMA infringement decision under the Competition Act 1998 from a Commission decision under Article 101 TFEU, you'll answer half your exam questions in the wrong jurisdiction.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 1 September 2026. Articles 101 and 102 TFEU are taught here as the analytical model UK competition law was built on and as EU law students should still recognise — they no longer apply directly to conduct in the UK. The Competition Act 1998 prohibitions (ss 2 and 18), by contrast, are current, in-force UK statute, enforced solely by the Competition and Markets Authority with no parallel EU jurisdiction since the end of the Brexit transition period. Where this lesson says 'the law', it specifies which regime it means.

parts.heading: Same law, two names: why this lesson is doubled
parts.voice: comparative — sets up the twin-track structure that runs through the whole lesson
body: Competition law rests on a simple worry: markets only deliver their benefits — lower prices, better products, innovation — if firms actually compete with each other rather than agreeing not to, or using market power to crush the firms that would otherwise compete with them.

The EU built two prohibitions around that worry: Article 101 TFEU catches anti-competitive agreements between firms (cartels, at the extreme); Article 102 TFEU catches abuse of a dominant position by a single powerful firm. Together they're the most-copied competition regime in the world.

The UK copied it directly. The Competition Act 1998 was drafted with the explicit aim of mirroring EU competition law almost provision for provision — s 2 tracks Article 101, s 18 tracks Article 102 — so that UK and EU competition law would develop in parallel. Since the end of the Brexit transition period, that parallel has broken: Articles 101 and 102 no longer apply directly to conduct in the UK, and the Competition and Markets Authority now enforces the domestic mirror alone. The structure is nearly identical; the jurisdiction is not.

components.definition: A UK statutory provision deliberately drafted to replicate an EU law rule's structure and language, so that UK courts and regulators could apply consistent principles — but which, post-Brexit, operates entirely under UK jurisdiction with no EU enforcement role.

interaction.prompt: Since the end of the Brexit transition period, who enforces UK competition law against a cartel operating only within the UK?
options: The Competition and Markets Authority alone, under the Competition Act 1998
The European Commission, under Article 101 TFEU, with the CMA assisting
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. There is no parallel EU jurisdiction over purely domestic UK conduct any more — the CMA applies the Competition Act 1998 on its own.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite — the European Commission has no jurisdiction over conduct confined to the UK post-Brexit. The CMA enforces the Competition Act 1998 alone, even though its provisions were drafted to mirror Articles 101 and 102 TFEU.

parts.heading: Article 101: agreements that shouldn't exist
parts.voice: structural — a reference part students will return to for the test
body: Article 101 TFEU prohibits agreements between undertakings, decisions by associations of undertakings, and concerted practices which may affect trade between Member States and which have as their object or effect the prevention, restriction or distortion of competition. That's a dense sentence, but three ideas carry the weight: there has to be some form of coordination between independent firms; it has to affect trade; and it has to restrict competition, either by its object (the obviously bad kind — price-fixing, market-sharing) or by its effect (subtler arrangements that turn out to harm competition once examined).

Consten and Grundig v Commission is the case that stretched 'agreement' wide. Grundig, a German electronics manufacturer, gave its French distributor Consten absolute territorial protection — no other distributor could sell Grundig products into France. The Court of Justice held this was caught by Article 101: an agreement doesn't need to be a formal cartel to restrict competition; partitioning the market along national lines is exactly the kind of restriction the provision targets, because it insulates distributors from competing with each other on price.

Object infringements — like price-fixing between competitors, or market-sharing agreements — are treated as so obviously harmful that no proof of actual anti-competitive effect is required. Effect infringements require the Commission (or, domestically, the CMA) to actually show the agreement harmed competition on the relevant market.

components.label: Article 101 TFEU — the elements
points: An agreement, decision by an association of undertakings, or concerted practice
Between independent undertakings (not within a single corporate group)
Which may affect trade between Member States
And has as its object OR effect the prevention, restriction or distortion of competition
Object infringements (e.g. price-fixing, market-sharing) need no proof of actual harm; effect infringements do

components.court: Court of Justice of the European Communities
components.factsShort: Grundig granted its French distributor Consten absolute territorial protection, blocking parallel imports of Grundig products from other Member States into France.
components.ratioShort: An agreement conferring absolute territorial protection restricts competition within Article 101, even between a manufacturer and a single distributor, because it prevents price competition between distributors of the same brand.

expanded.facts: Grundig, a German manufacturer, appointed Consten as its sole distributor in France and agreed to prevent its other distributors and wholesalers elsewhere in the Community from selling into French territory, giving Consten absolute protection from intra-brand competition. A French company, UNEF, began parallel importing Grundig products into France more cheaply; Consten sued for trade mark infringement, and the dispute reached the Commission, which found the distribution agreement infringed what is now Article 101.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Court of Justice upheld the Commission's finding, rejecting the argument that Article 101 only applied to horizontal agreements between competitors. Vertical agreements — between a manufacturer and its distributor — could restrict competition just as much, particularly where they eliminated all possibility of competition between the products of the same brand at the distribution level by sealing off national markets.
expanded.significance: This is the foundational case for reading 'agreement' broadly under Article 101 and for treating absolute territorial protection as an object restriction. It also underpins the single market principle that runs through EU competition law: agreements that recreate national trade barriers are treated with particular hostility, because they undermine market integration as well as competition.

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact in Consten and Grundig that made the arrangement an Article 101 problem, rather than an ordinary distribution deal.
interaction.scenarioText: Grundig appointed Consten as its sole distributor in France, then went further and prevented its distributors in other Member States from selling into French territory at all, blocking any possibility of parallel imports undercutting Consten's prices.
tappableSpans: appointed Consten as its sole distributor
prevented its distributors in other Member States from selling into French territory
blocking any possibility of parallel imports
interaction.correctSpan: prevented its distributors in other Member States from selling into French territory
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the restriction. A sole distributorship alone is common and lawful; sealing off the territory from all other sellers of the same brand is what converts it into an object restriction on competition.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: A single exclusive distributor isn't itself the problem — plenty of lawful agreements look like that. Look for the step that removes any possibility of competing sellers undercutting Consten within France.

parts.heading: Article 102: when power itself becomes the problem
parts.voice: case-narrative — builds the doctrine through the Hoffmann-La Roche facts
body: Article 101 needs two or more firms coordinating. Article 102 needs only one — but a powerful one. It prohibits any abuse by one or more undertakings of a dominant position within the internal market, in so far as it may affect trade between Member States.

Hoffmann-La Roche v Commission supplies the classic definition of dominance: a position of economic strength enjoyed by an undertaking which enables it to prevent effective competition being maintained on the relevant market, by affording it the power to behave to an appreciable extent independently of its competitors, customers and, ultimately, consumers. Roche, a pharmaceutical company with very high market shares across several vitamin markets, had tied customers into exclusive or near-exclusive purchasing through loyalty rebates — discounts that grew the more of their total requirements a customer bought from Roche.

The Court held those loyalty rebates were an abuse. Note what dominance is not: it is not itself unlawful to be dominant, and not itself unlawful to compete hard, even as a dominant firm. What Article 102 catches is the abuse — conduct that a dominant firm can get away with only because its market power insulates it from the normal competitive discipline that would punish the same conduct in a rival.

components.label: Article 102 TFEU — the elements
points: A dominant position — economic strength allowing the firm to act independently of competitors and customers
Held within the internal market or a substantial part of it
An abuse of that position — conduct a non-dominant firm could engage in freely, but which entrenches or exploits dominance when a dominant firm does it
Which may affect trade between Member States
Examples of abuse: exclusionary practices (loyalty rebates, predatory pricing, refusal to supply) and exploitative practices (excessive pricing, unfair terms)

components.court: Court of Justice of the European Communities
components.factsShort: Roche held very high market shares in several vitamin markets and gave customers loyalty rebates that increased the more of their total requirements they bought from Roche.
components.ratioShort: Loyalty-inducing rebates by a dominant firm are abusive under Article 102 because they tie customers by financial pressure rather than by competing on price or quality for each individual order.

expanded.facts: Hoffmann-La Roche held dominant positions, in some cases exceeding 80% market share, in several markets for vitamins used in food, pharmaceutical and other industries. It entered fidelity agreements with major customers offering rebates conditional on the customer buying all or most of its requirements from Roche, rather than a fixed discount for a fixed quantity.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Court of Justice held that fidelity rebates, which are conditional on the customer obtaining all or most of its requirements from the dominant undertaking, are incompatible with Article 102 because — unlike ordinary quantity discounts linked objectively to volume — they are designed to prevent customers from obtaining supplies from competing producers, and so deprive the customer of a choice of supply sources or restrict that choice.
expanded.significance: This case gives the leading definition of dominance and establishes the key distinction the exam will test: quantity rebates linked objectively to volume can be lawful, while loyalty or fidelity rebates that reward exclusivity are treated as abusive because they compete for the whole of a customer's demand through financial pressure rather than through merit.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that being dominant, by itself, is unlawful under Article 102 TFEU?
sliderLabels: Dominance alone is lawful — only its abuse is caught
interaction.explanation: Article 102 does not punish size or market power as such. A firm can lawfully hold and even strengthen a dominant position through genuine competition on the merits; what the provision catches is conduct — like Roche's loyalty rebates — that exploits or entrenches that dominance in a way a non-dominant firm could not.

parts.heading: The UK mirror: Competition Act 1998, ss 2 and 18
parts.voice: structural — a direct provision-by-provision mapping exercise
body: This is the part of the lesson that actually tells you the current law. The Competition Act 1998 contains two prohibitions drafted to track Articles 101 and 102 almost word for word, precisely so that decades of EU case law on the meaning of 'agreement', 'concerted practice', 'dominant position' and 'abuse' could guide UK interpretation.

Section 2 — the Chapter I prohibition — prohibits agreements between undertakings, decisions by associations of undertakings, or concerted practices which may affect trade within the United Kingdom and have as their object or effect the prevention, restriction or distortion of competition within the UK. Swap 'the United Kingdom' for 'Member States' and you have Article 101 again.

Section 18 — the Chapter II prohibition — prohibits any conduct by one or more undertakings which amounts to abuse of a dominant position in a market, if it may affect trade within the United Kingdom. Again, this is Article 102 with the geography changed.

The practical consequence: a cartel operating only within the UK today is a Competition Act 1998 s 2 matter, investigated and enforced by the CMA, with penalties of up to 10% of worldwide group turnover. It is not — cannot be — an Article 101 matter, because Article 101 no longer applies directly in the UK. The Consten and Grundig and Hoffmann-La Roche reasoning still matters, because UK courts and the CMA continue to draw on that body of case law when interpreting the near-identical domestic wording — but the authority enforcing it, and the statute being applied, are purely domestic.

components.text: Subject to section 3, agreements between undertakings, decisions by associations of undertakings or concerted practices which — (a) may affect trade within the United Kingdom, and (b) have as their object or effect the prevention, restriction or distortion of competition within the United Kingdom, are prohibited unless they are exempt in accordance with the provisions of this Part.
elements: Agreement, decision by an association, or concerted practice
May affect trade within the United Kingdom
Object or effect: prevention, restriction or distortion of competition within the United Kingdom

components.text: Subject to section 19, any conduct on the part of one or more undertakings which amounts to the abuse of a dominant position in a market is prohibited if it may affect trade within the United Kingdom.
elements: Conduct by one or more undertakings
Of a dominant position in a market
May affect trade within the United Kingdom

interaction.prompt: Compare Competition Act 1998 s 2(1) with Article 101 TFEU. What is the key structural difference between them?
options: The geographic scope: s 2 asks whether trade within the United Kingdom is affected, where Article 101 asks whether trade between Member States is affected — the substantive test for the agreement itself is otherwise near-identical
Section 2 requires proof of actual harm in every case, while Article 101 never does
Section 2 applies only to agreements between competitors, while Article 101 also covers unilateral conduct
interaction.explanation: The prohibitions were deliberately drafted in parallel. The only substantive difference that matters for identifying which regime applies is jurisdiction — UK trade under s 2, Member State trade under Article 101 — not the underlying test for what counts as an anti-competitive agreement.

parts.heading: Spotting the trap: which regime governs these facts?
parts.voice: direct — sets up the trap the tests will probe
body: The single most common mistake in this lesson is citing Article 101 or Article 102 as the operative law for a UK-only fact pattern set after the end of the transition period. It's an understandable mistake — the tests, the language, even most of the case law are shared — but it is a jurisdiction error, and examiners treat it as a serious one.

The fix is a habit, not a rule to memorise: before answering, ask what the geographic footprint of the conduct actually is. Conduct confined to the UK, investigated by the CMA, is a Competition Act 1998 matter — ss 2 and 18, full stop. Conduct that also affects trade between EU Member States and is investigated by the European Commission would be an EU law matter, governed by Articles 101 and 102 — but that's now genuinely rare from a UK vantage point, since a UK-based firm's purely UK conduct is outside EU jurisdiction entirely.

For most exam fact patterns in this module, the honest answer is: the doctrine is taught through Articles 101 and 102 and their case law because that's the analytical model and the historical source, but the operative law you'd actually cite for a live UK enforcement scenario is the Competition Act 1998 mirror.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often answer a scenario about a cartel operating entirely within the UK today by citing Article 101 TFEU and the Commission as the enforcer.
components.whyItsWrong: Article 101 TFEU has not applied directly to conduct in the UK since the end of the Brexit transition period, and the European Commission has no jurisdiction over conduct confined to the UK. The operative prohibition is Competition Act 1998 s 2, enforced by the CMA — even though the substantive test you'd apply is drawn from the same body of principle Article 101 established.

interaction.prompt: Two scenarios describing the same kind of conduct. Which one is currently governed by the Competition Act 1998 rather than Article 101 TFEU?
interaction.scenarioA: Two manufacturers based only in the UK, selling only to UK retailers, agree by telephone to fix the wholesale price of their products across England, Scotland and Wales.
interaction.scenarioB: A hypothetical question asking a student to explain, purely as a matter of legal history, how the Court of Justice characterised the Consten and Grundig distribution agreement in 1966.
interaction.explanation: Scenario A describes live UK-only conduct in 2026 — that is squarely a Competition Act 1998 s 2 matter for the CMA, not an Article 101 matter, because Article 101 no longer applies directly here. Scenario B is legal history: you'd still correctly cite Article 101 TFEU and Consten and Grundig, because you're describing what the EU law said and did at the time, not applying live law to live UK conduct.

testPool.prompt: Name the two TFEU articles that form the classical EU-law model for competition law, and briefly state what each prohibits.
acceptableAnswers: article 101 anti-competitive agreements, article 102 abuse of dominance
testPool.modelAnswer: Article 101 TFEU prohibits agreements, decisions and concerted practices between undertakings that restrict competition; Article 102 TFEU prohibits abuse of a dominant position by one or more undertakings.

testPool.prompt: Which UK statute contains the domestic prohibitions mirroring Articles 101 and 102 TFEU?
options: The Competition Act 1998
The European Communities Act 1972

testPool.prompt: Which body currently enforces the Competition Act 1998 prohibitions against conduct confined to the UK?
options: The Competition and Markets Authority, acting alone
The European Commission, with the CMA acting as its delegate
The Court of Justice of the European Union, sitting as first instance
testPool.trapExplanation: There is no EU enforcement role over purely UK conduct post-Brexit, and the CMA is not a delegate of the Commission — it is the sole domestic regulator applying UK statute under UK jurisdiction.

testPool.prompt: Under Competition Act 1998 s 18, is it necessary to prove that a firm intended to abuse its dominant position?
options: No — s 18 focuses on the effect and character of the conduct, not the firm's subjective intent
Yes — abuse requires proof of a deliberate anti-competitive intent

testPool.prompt: Competition Act 1998 s 2(1)(a) requires that an agreement 'may affect trade within the United Kingdom'. What is the closest equivalent requirement in Article 101 TFEU?
options: That the agreement may affect trade between Member States
That the agreement must involve at least three undertakings
That the agreement must be in writing

testPool.prompt: In the passage below adapted from Hoffmann-La Roche, highlight the sentence that defines dominance.
testPool.passage: The undertaking held very high market shares across several vitamin markets. Dominance is a position of economic strength enjoyed by an undertaking which enables it to prevent effective competition being maintained on the relevant market, by affording it the power to behave to an appreciable extent independently of its competitors, customers and, ultimately, consumers. The loyalty rebates it offered were found to be abusive.
testPool.ratioSentence: Dominance is a position of economic strength enjoyed by an undertaking which enables it to prevent effective competition being maintained on the relevant market, by affording it the power to behave to an appreciable extent independently of its competitors, customers and, ultimately, consumers.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario better illustrates an object restriction under Article 101, rather than an effect restriction requiring proof of actual market harm?
testPool.scenarioA: Three competing UK manufacturers agree by secret meeting to fix the minimum price at which they will each sell a product.
testPool.scenarioB: A manufacturer imposes a maximum resale price on its distributor, which economists later dispute actually reduced overall competition.
testPool.explanation: Price-fixing between competitors is a classic object restriction — no proof of actual effect is required because the restriction on competition is inherent in the agreement itself. Scenario B is the kind of case where effect would need to be examined.

testPool.prompt: Put these developments in Article 101's relationship with UK law in chronological order.
items: Article 101 TFEU (and its predecessors) binds the UK via EU membership
The Competition Act 1998 is enacted, mirroring Articles 101 and 102 in domestic law
The UK leaves the EU and the Brexit transition period ends
Article 101 TFEU ceases to apply directly to conduct in the UK; the Competition Act 1998 prohibitions continue, enforced solely by the CMA

testPool.prompt: Two UK-based haulage companies, operating only within England, agree by email to divide up regional customers between themselves so neither will bid for the other's clients. Which regime currently governs this conduct?
options: Competition Act 1998 s 2, enforced by the CMA
Article 101 TFEU, enforced by the European Commission
Neither regime applies because the agreement was made by email rather than in person
testPool.explanation: This is UK-only conduct with no cross-border EU element, so the Competition Act 1998 s 2 prohibition applies and the CMA has jurisdiction. Article 101 TFEU has no application here post-Brexit.

testPool.prompt: A dominant UK supermarket chain offers a rebate to a supplier's wholesale customers that only applies if the customer buys at least 95% of its total stock from that chain, rather than a fixed discount for a fixed order size. Applying the Hoffmann-La Roche reasoning (now via the Competition Act 1998 mirror), is this likely to be treated as abusive?
options: Yes — it is a loyalty/fidelity rebate that ties customers by financial pressure rather than rewarding genuine volume, mirroring the rebates condemned in Hoffmann-La Roche
No — any rebate offered by a dominant firm is automatically lawful because discounts benefit consumers
No — rebates can only be abusive if the dominant firm also refuses to supply competitors entirely
testPool.explanation: The 95%-of-requirements structure mirrors the fidelity rebates in Hoffmann-La Roche: it is not linked objectively to volume but to exclusivity, deterring the customer from sourcing from rivals. Under the current UK regime this reasoning would be applied via Competition Act 1998 s 18.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that would make this a Chapter I (s 2) rather than a Chapter II (s 18) matter.
testPool.scenarioText: A dominant national retailer and three of its independent suppliers hold a meeting and jointly agree to fix the minimum shelf price at which the suppliers' goods will be sold across all UK stores.
testPool.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The presence of coordination between multiple undertakings — an agreement — is what triggers s 2 (mirroring Article 101), regardless of whether one of the parties also happens to be dominant.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the fact showing more than one undertaking coordinating conduct, rather than a single firm acting unilaterally — that's what distinguishes a s 2 (agreement) issue from a s 18 (unilateral abuse) issue.

testPool.prompt: A UK-only online retailer holds an 85% share of the market for a niche product and refuses to supply a smaller competitor's warehouse with stock, despite having spare capacity and no legitimate commercial reason for the refusal. The smaller competitor cannot obtain the product elsewhere and is forced out of business. Analyse whether the retailer has infringed UK competition law, and identify which statutory provision applies.
factsToOrder: The retailer holds an 85% market share
The retailer refuses to supply a smaller competitor despite spare capacity
There is no legitimate commercial reason for the refusal
The competitor cannot obtain the product elsewhere and is forced out of business
All conduct is confined to the UK

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the retailer has abused a dominant position by refusing to supply, and which UK provision governs conduct confined entirely to the UK.
modelAnswer.rule: Competition Act 1998 s 18 (mirroring Article 102 TFEU and the Hoffmann-La Roche definition of dominance) prohibits abuse of a dominant position where it may affect trade within the UK; an unjustified refusal to supply by a dominant firm, which forecloses a competitor without legitimate commercial justification, is a recognised category of exclusionary abuse.
modelAnswer.application: An 85% market share strongly indicates dominance — the retailer can act independently of competitive pressure. The refusal to supply, despite spare capacity and absent any legitimate commercial reason, forecloses the smaller competitor entirely and forces it from the market — a hallmark exclusionary abuse. Because all the conduct is confined to the UK, the operative law is the Competition Act 1998 mirror, enforced by the CMA, not Article 102 TFEU.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The retailer has likely infringed Competition Act 1998 s 18 by abusing its dominant position through an unjustified refusal to supply; Article 102 TFEU has no application here post-Brexit even though its case law informs the analysis.

testPool.prompt: A student writes: 'Because Competition Act 1998 s 2 was drafted to mirror Article 101 TFEU, UK courts must still refer questions about its interpretation to the Court of Justice of the European Union.' What is wrong with this statement?
options: Nothing — mirrored provisions always require a CJEU reference
The mirroring explains why UK courts may still draw on EU case law for guidance, but there is no ongoing obligation or ability to refer questions to the CJEU post-Brexit
Section 2 was not in fact drafted to mirror Article 101 at all
testPool.trapExplanation: Structural similarity between the domestic and EU provisions does not create any live jurisdictional link — UK courts can no longer make Article 267 TFEU references at all, on any subject, since the end of the transition period. They may still find pre-exit CJEU case law persuasive, but that is a matter of choice, not obligation.

testPool.prompt: A UK exam question describes conduct occurring entirely within the UK in 2026 and asks which body would investigate it. Is 'the European Commission' ever the correct answer for such a scenario?
options: No — post-Brexit, the Commission has no jurisdiction over conduct confined to the UK; the CMA investigates under the Competition Act 1998
Yes — the Commission retains a residual power to investigate any conduct within a former Member State

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The recurring mistake in this lesson is citing Article 101 or Article 102 TFEU as the operative law for present-day UK-only conduct. Treat the TFEU articles as the analytical model and historical source; treat Competition Act 1998 ss 2 and 18, enforced by the CMA, as the law you'd actually cite for a live UK scenario.
